💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Sources indicate that dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:.

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”.

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

It has been revealed that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. Tech Report: 60 mindful New Year's resolution ideas to try in 2027

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some Upcoming Year’s resolutions.
  • Then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

We’ve all been there. January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some Upcoming Year’s resolutions. You might optimistically think, “You know what? I’m going to be healthier this year! I’m only going to drink on the weekends.”.

Then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine. You’re instantly filled with regret for breaking your resolution and vow to never do them again because they don’t work and are clearly designed to make you feel disappointed.

Take a deep breath. Resolutions don’t have to be this substantial set up for failure that feel impossible to keep. They can be as big or as small as you want them to be. We’ve put together a list of 60 mindful resolutions that are less about striving for perfection or making huge changes in your life, and more about slowly helping you to grow and build better habits in an achievable way. Sounds nice, right?

So let’s ditch our list of impossible goals and jump into 60 resolutions that could help you thrive in 2027.

Industry observers note that at the end of the year, many of us step back and realize that we feel really disconnected from a lot of the people in our life. We get busy and stuck in our own little world. It’s too easy for connections with our family, friends, partners, or coworkers to dwindle from time to time.

It has been revealed that if this sounds familiar, here are 15 resolutions that can help you build more fulfilling relationships so that your support networks are there for you when you need it. (And you’re there for them when they need it too.).

Pro tip: you don’t need to do all of 15. Just try choosing a few that feel good to you and then take some small steps towards adding them into your routine.

Recent findings suggest that make a habit of giving your full attention to the people who matter most to you. Try planning regular (or semi-regular) family dinners, date nights, or hangs with friends. If you like phone calls, those work great too. (Just make sure you’re fully present!).

When someone’s talking to you, focus fully on what they’re saying instead of thinking about your reply or what you’re going to eat for your next meal (we’ve all been there). Active listening reveals respect to your loved one and can help deepen your bond. If you want to get better at active listening, here are eight techniques to help.

Too often, we take those around us for granted, so let the people in your life know you appreciate them. Saying something as easy as, “thank you” or writing a cute little note can let your loved one know how much they mean to you and make them feel good. Who doesn’t want to make their loved one feel good?

If you love them, say it. Life’s too short! Telling someone you love them is powerful and can help you grow a stronger bond. If you have people in your life like a macho uncle or disengaged cousin who have a hard time saying I love you, be the first to jump in and show them that it’s okay to express your affection for one another.

If you notice someone struggling in your life, step in and help. It doesn't need to be revolutionary. It could be helping with laundry or simply being there to listen. Just letting them know that you see their efforts and want to help can make a huge difference.

Relationships are work. And in order for them to work, you need to put time into them. So set a reminder to check in with your loved ones, especially the ones you don’t see often. A quick text or call can do the trick and help you stay connected with your favorite people. And if you have folks in your life who are struggling, or who experience loneliness, make an extra effort to reach out and show you care.

Recent findings suggest that don’t let misunderstandings grow. When you’re upset with someone, bring it up to them calmly and kindly, and with the goal of finding a solution. It can help to lead with “I feel” statements. And if your feelings are hurt over an innocent misunderstanding, start with, “I know you didn’t mean to hurt my feelings but,” so the other person knows they’re not in trouble and you want to come to a place of understanding.

It has been revealed that this might sound obvious, but if your loved one has good news, show genuine excitement for the good things that are happening for them. We all feel good when others celebrate with us. So send those flowers — almost no one’s going to get mad at you for sending flowers. Sometimes celebrating success for others feels hard if you feel stuck in your life, but by genuinely finding happiness for others, you may feel the glow of that happiness yourself.

It has been revealed that use conversions with others as a time to genuinely disconnect from technology and focus on being together. When you’re spending time with someone, keep your phone in your pocket, in your purse, or somewhere that’s not in your hand. Give your loved one your full attention. This will make them feel seen and it helps you to stay more in the moment and form deeper connections.

In a recent development, everyone loves to feel seen and valued. Sometimes just surprising someone you love with a small gesture can make their day. It doesn’t have to be major, it could just be showing up to a hang with your loved one’s favorite snack, their preferred coffee drink, or even a small bouquet of flowers. Trying to be better about budgeting? Handwritten cards, or homemade crafts also make lovely surprises.

It has been revealed that when someone you care about is struggling, before reacting, take a moment to put yourself in their shoes and understand what they might be going through. This can be a lot easier mentioned than done, but try to treat them the way you would want to be treated —  with kindness instead of judgment.

💙 If Empathy doesn’t come easy for you, check out this meditation from Tamara Levitt’s Relationships with Others series.

We all have preferences for how we like to give and receive love and it’s so special when the people in our lives make an effort to communicate affection in the ways we most appreciate. So take some time to understand a partner, family member, or friends love languages (here’s an overview of all five and how to identify yours). Showing love in the ways they like can make you closer. (And probably earn you brownie points!).

Sources indicate that say yes to an invite or an activity you wouldn’t normally do. Stepping out of your comfort zone can help you feel energized and open you up to new experiences and learnings about yourself. The one time when it’s okay not to say yes is if you’re establishing boundaries with your emotional energy or time. It’s all about balance!

In a recent development, while saying yes is great (see above), saying no is also crucial. Make an effort to have healthy relationships with solid boundaries. Tell people what you need, like alone time or limits on work talk. And respect their boundaries too. If all of that sounds tough, check out these six tips to setting healthy boundaries in your relationships.

Humans make mistakes and the best thing you can do is to acknowledge them, learn and grow. So try to take responsibility if you make a mistake. You’ll feel free of guilt and you won’t have to double down on something you probably didn’t mean to do in the first place (like a bad joke that hurt someone’s feelings, or a meeting you were super late for.) A heartfelt apology can mend any damage and show your maturity (these seven tips will help you do it).

According to recent reports, doesn’t it feel like we’re always trying to find a better work-life balance, get promoted, improve our work ethic, and feel more fulfilled with the work we’re doing? That constant desire for some sort of growth or change can be overwhelming and leave you not knowing where to start.

So we’ve put together 15 work resolutions that might be more sustainable and rewarding for you — and will hopefully make the whole process feel less overwhelming.

Recent findings suggest that protecting your personal time is so notable for avoiding burnout, so decide on clear work hours and stick to them. Try setting a goal for logging off by 6pm or not looking at emails in your off time. If your job doesn’t presently give you the freedom to set these boundaries, chat with your superiors and express your goals where work-life balance is concerned.

Sources indicate that organize your workspace to reduce clutter. A working area that you like (or at least doesn’t cause more stress) can really improve your mood and your focus. Once you reduce the clutter and get rid of any items that aren’t sparking joy, you could mindfully add things that feel good like a plant, photo, or a comfy chair.

It has been revealed that large projects can be overwhelming. Try breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps to make them less daunting and help you stay on track. You can also practice time-boxing to keep your focus — here’s how to do it .

It has been revealed that go for a five-minute walk, enjoy a cup or tea, or do a quick stretch. It doesn’t really matter what you do on a break, just that you do something to rest your mind and give your body a little love. Set reminders if it’ll help you remember. (Here are 20 ways to take a mindful break.).

Start each day by identifying your top three priorities. If you focus on the most key tasks first, this will help you make progress where it matters most. Got a few things on your to-do list that aren’t time sensitive? Resist the temptation to try to get them done when you’re exhausted and bump them to tomorrow when you can focus.

According to recent reports, just like you want to celebrate the achievements of the people in your life, it’s equally important to celebrate yourself! Take note of all of your accomplishments. This can help boost your confidence, help you stay motivated, and even make you smile.

Making new friends isn’t just for your school years. Make an effort to connect with coworkers or other people in your field. Getting coffee with colleagues can help you build relationships and even help with career growth. You might find that your career is more fulfilling when you have solid relationships with colleagues and coworkers.

Work on being clear and concise in emails, meetings, and in conversations. Practicing good communication not only improves your productivity but also helps avoid misunderstandings (these 13 tips can help).

According to recent reports, if you’re overwhelmed and juggling too much, look for tasks that can be given to others to make your life easier. This doesn’t mean you’re not good at your job. It just means you're making sure your energy is spent where it’s needed most.

Industry observers note that struggling to focus? Single-tasting is where it’s at. Take on one task at a time and not five at once. This will improve the quality of your work and help you feel less like you want to scream.

It has been revealed that even if it’s scary, seek out feedback from your boss, coworkers, or clients. Constructive input can help you get better and show that you want to improve. Just make sure you’re also receiving feedback for things you’re doing well, not just areas where you could do better.

In a recent development, find a method that helps you stay on top of deadlines. A to-do list app, a daily planner, or a bullet journal could help keep track of all your tasks. Explore some different ideas to find what works best for you.

Don’t hesitate to ask for what you need. If anything, this can help you get taken more seriously and help with career growth. Ask for that raise, request that more flexible schedule, tell your boss you need additional resources to complete that project.

💙 Learn how to practice Speaking Up at work with this session from the Mindful Leadership Wisdom Series.

In a recent development, set goals that align with your long-term dreams and values, not just what you hope to achieve. These could be around building confidence, becoming a more mindful leader, or exploring a upcoming field you’ve always been interested in.

In a recent development, when you don’t feel mentally like you’re firing on all cylinders, it can be tough to even think of what to focus on to help your mental health. We get it — you’re probably already stressed, so making a decision on a resolution to be less stressed might be the last thing you want to (or can) do.

To help you out, we put together a list of 15 small and intentional resolutions that will help nurture your mind and create space for calm and joy in 2027.

(Psst: You don’t have to do all of them. Start with one or two that’ll help you feel more balanced, calm, and connected, and then go from there.).

According to recent reports, write down and reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and experiences each day. This can help you process your emotions and recognize some patterns you have. Journaling is also a great way to practice gratitude.

Each day, take a moment to think of three things you’re grateful for. This can rewire your brain to look for the positives in your life. It doesn’t have to be getting a promotion or finding your perfect partner, it can be as small as not burning your bagel today. If you want to find more ways to incorporate gratitude into your days, here are eight ideas to get you started.

Spend a few minutes a day practicing mindfulness. And while this could be a five minute meditation, it could also be a bit of deep breathing on a work break, or just noticing the sights and sounds on your morning walk. Any moment where you become fully present counts!

Recent findings suggest that go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help you get better quality sleep (here are six more tips to help you get those Zzzzs). The more rested you are, the more you’ll be able to handle the stress that comes up throughout the day.

Sources indicate that nature has a way of calming us down and recharging us, so if it’s possible, try to get outside everyday. It doesn't have to be a massive hike, it can be as simple as walking around your block or even just going into your yard.

This is a big one! Try to gradually reduce the time you spend on your phone, computer, or watching TV, especially before bed. You could read that novel that’s been on your bedside table for ever or catch up with a loved one instead. But take it slow, we know it’s not easy.

Give yourself permission to say no to things that overwhelm or overcommit you. It’s more vital to protect your energy than to burn yourself out trying to please other people. If saying no is hard for you, here’s 30 ways to do it nicely.

Get in the habit of reaching out to a loved one or a therapist when you’re feeling stressed or overwhelmed. Talking about our feelings can help us feel lighter and even give us a upcoming perspective.

It has been revealed that A clean environment isn’t just for your desk. Having a clean home can calm you too. So take some small steps to organize your home. You might try doing just one room at a time, it doesn’t need to be all at once.

Schedule regular breaks so you don’t have a meltdown. These pauses can really help you reduce your stress and keep you focused. Grabbing a glass of water, breathing deeply, or gently stretching can all help reset you and give your mind a moment to rest.

Sources indicate that treat yourself the way you would your closest friend. Avoid going in on yourself with harsh, critical thoughts and instead say some sweet nothings to yourself. We know this isn’t always easy, so here are eight tips to help you quiet that inner critic.

Start a hobby that lets you express yourself. This can be therapeutic and put you in a better mood. Ever been curious about painting or playing music? Maybe now’s your chance to explore that curiosity.

Industry observers note that exercising relieves a lot of stress. But you don’t need to spend hours at the gym or set some big weight loss goal. Instead, try out a fresh yoga class, have a dance party in your living room, or find other ways to move your body that feel nourishing to you.

Go easy on yourself, you don’t need to be perfect (newsflash: there’s no such thing). It can help to focus on all the small ways you're growing each day, not on the destination. Sometimes it’s better to think about growth-setting instead of goal setting.

According to recent reports, don’t regularly spend your time on something that drains your energy. Seek out places that bring you positivity instead. If certain people you hang around with make you feel bad, limit your exposure to them. This might look like setting boundaries with family about how many events you attend each year, or with friends by limiting how much you talk or get together.

In a recent development, 💙 If you’re looking for more positivity in your life, learn how to Process and Move Past Negativity during the Overcome Stress and Anxiety series with Dr. Julie Smith.

Recent findings suggest that okay, let’s face it. Most of us want to look and feel our best — and there’s nothing wrong with that. But better physical health is also about feeling energized, staying strong, and giving our body the help it needs to thrive.

It has been revealed that we don’t need to tell you that working out consistently is a lot easier said than done. Sure, in a perfect world, we always have the time and energy to get to the gym. But we don’t live in that world. We have endless responsibilities and working out might be the first thing to go when we’re busy.

So explore these 15 manageable resolutions that can help you feel strong and energized going into 2027. And remember, you don’t need to force yourself to go all-in on physical wellness to feel better. Just start with one or two that feel like they’d be easier to make a consistent habit and go from there.

Aim for some form of movement every day –– it doesn’t have to be intense. Try a 10–minute stretch or a brisk walk through your favorite part of your neighborhood. Focus on what makes you feel good in your body, which may change day to day.

Sources indicate that hydration makes you feel good and stay alert, so try to aim for 8–10 glasses of water a day. Carry a reusable water bottle with you to make it easier to hit your goal and remind you to drink. If regular water feels boring try adding slices of your favorite citrus or fresh mint to your water.

Add a rainbow of foods to your plate! Focus on eating a mix of fruits, veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains. Try meal prepping ahead of time to make it easier for you to choose healthy options. Bonus points if you try to stay mindful while you cook and while you eat — here’s how.

Swap out processed snacks for healthier options like fruit, nuts, seeds, or yogurt. Try keeping nutritious snacks nearby to make it easier to avoid reaching your favorite sweets. With that in mind, don’t forget that dark chocolate has some antioxidants so adding a few dark chocolate chips to your trail mix is a-okay with us!

When you sleep better, you feel better. End of story. Aim for around eight hours of quality sleep each night. It can help to have a wind down routine at the end of your day to help your body know that it’s time for rest. These nine steps can help you create a calming bedtime routine.

If you are able to take stairs instead of elevators or escalators, go for it! Making small, active choices throughout your day to help you get a little more movement. You could also try parking farther away to get in a few extra steps.

Add some stretching into your daily routine to improve your flexibility, reduce your tension, and prevent injuring yourself. Try stretching for a few minutes as soon as you get out of bed or right before you get into bed — here are seven we like.

We know it can be frustrating or scary to go see a doctor, but don’t wait to see one until you feel sick. Set up your physicals and dental cleanings so that you can breathe easy and not worry about your health. You’ll be proud of yourself when you leave that doctor’s office!

Generally, it’s recommended to cut back on foods high in sugar. You may be surprised how much sugar some of your daily go-tos have, so stay mindful of what you’re consuming (you could check the labels for sugar content if that works for you).. It’s not about never having a treat, but bringing more awareness to what you’re eating and how it’s making you feel. It’s all about balance.

Sources indicate that working out can really feel like work a lot of the time. So shake up your routine to help keep you excited to exercise. Ever tried kickboxing or swimming? Maybe 2027 is the year you hop in the boxing ring or jump in the pool.

In a recent development, if you have a desk job, try to stand up and move every hour. Consider switching to a standing desk if that’s an option. If you work from home and have space for a walking pad in front of a standing desk you can also get your steps in while you work.

We know that the latest year isn’t always the time you want to get outside for a walk, but sunshine and time in nature can boost your mood. If you live in the northern hemisphere, bundle up and try going for a walk, run, or bike ride outside whenever the weather allows it.

If you drink alcohol, consider cutting back by a few drinks or setting limits. It can help to have fun or festive swap, so try sipping on flavored sparkling water or a mocktail at a social event or as a treat at the end of a long week. Sometimes creating a special drink that’s free of booze creates the same excitement as making a special cocktail. And you might love the way you feel the next morning when you’re hydrating your body with your evening beverage instead of dehydrating it.

It has been revealed that good posture helps prevent back and neck pain so pay attention to how you sit and stand. And add exercises that focus on strengthening your core into your workout. This will help support better alignment. Sitting at a desk for work? Set alarms every so often to remind you to stand up and stretch.

It has been revealed that celebrating your progress helps you to keep going — we all need a good pat on the back. If you drink an extra glass of water or walk an extra mile, take note of it. Maybe even do a little happy dance. If you go for a walk four days in a row, make a note in your journal or notebook. The more you celebrate your progress the prouder of yourself you’ll be (and the easier it is to keep it up).

💙 Learn how to celebrate the Small Wins on the path to achieving your larger goals with help from Jay Shetty.

Sources indicate that latest Year’s resolutions are personal goals or promises you make to yourself at the start of a new year. They can be about anything and it’s entirely up to you. They can be big like training for a marathon or small like drinking more water.

Usually people use it as a chance to reflect, change up some patterns in their life, and start fresh. If you’re looking to set a resolution but don’t know where to start, here are five areas people tend to focus on:.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to make resolutions to have a wonderful fresh year. But if you want to try, keep in mind that resolutions work best when you make them work for you. So yes — resolutions matter if you use them as a tool to help you live with more purpose and joy, then you’ll set yourself up for more success.

It has been revealed that when you’re setting your resolutions, focus on what would make you feel happier, healthier and more fulfilled and go from there. And approach resolutions with kindness and flexibility, especially if you don’t end up following through on one.

If the idea of resolutions feels overwhelming — we get it. Here’s three ways that could make it easier for you:.

Focus on one word or theme for the year that feels right to you, like “balance” or “growth.”.

Set a small monthly intention instead of a year-long commitment.

Celebrate progress instead of perfection by noticing little wins along the way.

In a recent development, we wish there were five magical resolutions that could solve all of our problems at once. But unfortunately there’s no such thing. What we can tell you is the most successful resolutions tend to be the ones that feel right to you.

Sources indicate that it’s important to focus on the right area when setting your resolution, so you’ll be more likely to stick with them. Here are five areas to focus on when setting your resolution:.

Resolutions that focus on building stronger relationships — Pick ones that’ll fill you up and add more joy to your life.

Resolutions that focus on taking care of your physical health — Pick ones that focus on regular exercise, better nutrition, or improved sleep.

Resolutions that focus on your mental health — Pick ones that practice gratitude or mindfulness, so that they can help you feel calmer and more balanced.

Resolutions that focus on your career –– Pick ones that focus on learning a fresh skill or creating a better work-life balance so that your professional life can become more rewarding.

Resolutions that focus on personal growth –– Pick ones that focus on starting latest hobbies or giving back to your community.

It has been revealed that all of us at one point or another have probably failed at a resolution we’ve set for ourselves. And when that happens, it can feel pretty disappointing. But resolutions can work — if you set them in the right way.

Resolutions that are vague or overly ambitious tend to be a recipe for failure. But if you set ones that are realistic and meaningful to you, it’ll be a lot easier to keep your resolution and see the change you want. But remember to be flexible and kind to yourself. We’re all not perfect and mistakes happen. So try not to beat yourself up if you don’t stick to your goals perfectly. Focus on progress, not perfection.

It has been revealed that if you find it easier to set monthly intentions as opposed to setting one year-long resolution, go for that. Tailor the resolutions so they work best for you.

Sometimes the minute we think of resolutions, we can get sad or overwhelmed at the baggage of our past failed resolutions. If this is you — we understand. Resolutions aren’t for everyone. But if you’re interested, there are other ways you can focus on self-improvement and growth.

If a long list of goals is too daunting for you, try picking a single word to guide your year. You could use words like “balance,” or “connection,” to remind yourself to make choices that match with your values.

If setting smaller, short-term goals might help you to stay motivated, you could try focusing on building better sleep habits in January, and then shifting to something like improving your diet in February.

Industry observers note that if tracking your progress will make it more fun for you and help you to invest more, try using a habit tracker app, or even just a calendar. This way it’ll be easier to celebrate your little wins along the way.

Industry observers note that resolutions that focus on relationships can bring more connection, understanding, and happiness into your life. And a good way to show the people you love the most how much they mean to you is to set a resolution to spend more quality time with them.

Acts of kindness also go a long way to strengthen your relationships. So if this is vital to you, try setting an intention to express gratitude more often, like thanking your partner for their support.

In a recent development, you could also set a resolution to unplug more often. This can help free up your time and create more meaningful, distraction-free moments with the people you care about the most.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.
  • According to recent reports, the Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which unveiled aims in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years.
  • In a recent development, the UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.

According to recent reports, the Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which unveiled aims in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.

In a recent development, the UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport mentioned that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).

The painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, notes an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.

The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.

Recent findings suggest that founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting.
  • While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.
  • According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research demonstrates emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”.

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

It has been revealed that lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

According to recent reports, JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so crucial for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s key for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”.

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It notes “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

It has been revealed that JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

Sources indicate that but pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”.

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Industry observers note that ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

In a recent development, instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”.

Sources indicate that the interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

Recent findings suggest that LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sources indicate that sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

In a recent development, juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the fresh book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that london bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It states something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical latest works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.

According to recent reports, in Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.

It has been revealed that “She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is important to add more images and visual representation,” she remarked.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, Fresh York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is right now having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.

Nicole Eisenman's Stack (2022-24), installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy.

Recent findings suggest that photo: Damien Griffiths. © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the artist and Hauser & Wirth.

According to recent reports, at its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.

Sources indicate that barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s New York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.

Recent findings suggest that eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.

In strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

#103425. Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food.
  • News spreads like wildfire across the camp.
  • Industry observers note that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

News spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

Industry observers note that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

Industry observers note that insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

According to recent reports, anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

It has been revealed that like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Sources indicate that gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

No society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

Recent findings suggest that our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

Industry observers note that A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

Industry observers note that ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

It has been revealed that like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

In a recent development, egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

In a recent development, you open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

Recent findings suggest that before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

The best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:.

What do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

In a recent development, how much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

How personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

Sources indicate that what's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

Calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

Industry observers note that content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. Personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

Standout feature: For us, it's the sleep content. Sleep Stories are the first thing we’d recommend to a friend who’s struggling with sleep.

Sources indicate that headspace is another widely-used meditation app, and it leans into teaching. Many sessions are organized into courses that walk you through a topic step by step.

Industry observers note that content library: The app features beginner courses and SOS meditations, short sessions for when stress spikes. It also has themed collections for focus and movement. For sleep, there are Sleepcasts.

Personalization: Headspace offers personalized recommendations and its AI companion, Ebb, lets you talk through how you’re feeling and suggests app content in response.

Standout feature: We like how Headspace gives beginners a clear path to follow, starting with its 10-session Basics course.

Insight Timer started as a meditation timer and grew into a large library of guided meditations, with plenty of free content and a paid tier called MemberPlus.

Content library: The app hosts a catalog of meditations, talks, and music tracks, plus a meditation timer for people who prefer to sit in silence.

Personalization: You can join teacher-led challenges to help you stay on track, and the streak feature tracks how many days in a row you’ve meditated.

Sources indicate that standout feature: We like how much the app offers for free. With so much available, you can try a range of teachers before paying for anything.

Calm won’t be right for everyone, but here’s why we love it. (Keep in mind that this section is our point of view, not a neutral comparison.).

It has been revealed that we’ve also produced a lot of quick meditations over the past few years, all under five minutes. So even the busiest person, or the most skeptical first-timer, has something small to try.

According to recent reports, then there’s how the app looks and feels. The visuals lean into calming nature—think misty forests, rain on a window, slow ocean waves—so opening the app itself sets the scene for calm. And if you just need to tune out the world for a while, our Rain on Leaves soundscape is a legit vibe.

In a recent development, the numbers back up the impact. More than 180 million people worldwide have downloaded Calm, and its content has been studied in peer-reviewed research. For example, in one randomized trial of 88 stressed college students, those who used Calm for eight weeks reported lower perceived stress than a wait-list group.

In a recent development, they may help, though the research is still young. An updated review of 45 randomized trials found improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms among people using mindfulness apps, compared with control groups. The effects were modest, and the authors note we still need larger, higher-quality studies to say how much apps help and for whom.

It has been revealed that an app also isn’t a substitute for professional care. If you’re struggling with your mental health, it’s worth talking to a doctor, who can help you find the right support.

Yes, though how much is free varies a lot. Calm and Headspace each offer a limited selection of free sessions plus a free trial of their paid plans, with most of the library behind a subscription. Insight Timer works the other way around: the bulk of its catalog is free, with a paid MemberPlus tier for extras like courses and offline listening.

Recent findings suggest that to choose the right meditation app, start with your main goal, whether that’s stress relief, better sleep, or a guided start as a beginner. From there, check prices and any features you care about, like offline listening or language options. Then take advantage of the free trials. Most apps offer one, and it’s a good way to see how an app fits before you pay. While you’re trying it out, sample a few different narrators. A lot of meditation comes down to the voice guiding you, and finding someone you connect with can turn the practice into something you look forward to.

Calm is worth it if you want to ease stress and anxiety, sleep better, focus when your mind wanders, or learn the basics of meditation. The app may be a helpful way to build a daily mental health habit, with support for moments from a racing mind at bedtime to a hard day at work. Whether you need quick relief in the moment or ongoing support through a life change, Calm is for you.

You can try a 7-day free trial to see how it fits your flow, and you don’t need to know which content format you prefer ahead of time.

On Calm, you’ll find hundreds of Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, daily meditations from a rotating cast of instructors, music, soundscapes, and Emergency Calm sessions for high-stress moments. On Headspace, you’ll find a more course-led, step-by-step approach and an AI companion called Ebb. Both offer free content and a free trial, so the best way to decide is to try each and see which feels right for you.

Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852.
  • The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back.
  • “What happened this July was really special,” states George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

“What happened this July was really special,” states George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke states. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker says. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

Recent findings suggest that things moved rapidly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.

It has been revealed that after the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree states, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker notes, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts showed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results showed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Recent findings suggest that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)
