#103336. How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate.
  • According to recent reports, while most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly released, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years.
  • Industry observers note that frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while looks continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.

According to recent reports, while most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly released, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.

Industry observers note that frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh. “It’s a marriage,” Nusseibeh claims about the fair’s partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism. “And the fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding” Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi.

According to recent reports, regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.

This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.

Industry observers note that "We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market.".

That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh states, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.

Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the firm following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”.

According to recent reports, frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open on 11 December, is in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District Courtesy the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the tech giant run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a newly introduced company founded by Emanuel called Mari.

Recent findings suggest that mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of the DCT’s chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

In a recent development, this multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's aims align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.

Zayed National Museum opened in December 2025 Courtesy Zayed National Museum.

The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.

It has been revealed that how measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no intends to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.

Sources indicate that the luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

In a recent development, stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

In a recent development, the fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

#103335. Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep

Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that what if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move?
  • It has been revealed that the findings suggest that consistency could be an vital but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep.
  • The study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that what if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move? Research from The University of Texas at Austin suggests that being physically active every day, even for short periods, may help people spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep that support recovery, mood, and mental health.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that consistency could be an vital but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep. Rather than saving all their workouts for the weekend, people may benefit from making movement a regular part of their daily routines.

The study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months. While previous studies have largely examined how much time people spend exercising, the researchers focused on a different question: Does the number of days someone exercises influence how well they sleep?

Recent findings suggest that "We wanted to know whether it matters if someone spreads out their exercise over the week versus doing it all at once, like a 'weekend warrior,'" stated Benjamin Baird, a research assistant professor of psychology in UT Austin's College of Liberal Arts. "And for sleep health, frequency does seem to matter.".

Just 10 Minutes of Daily Exercise May Improve Deep Sleep.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that participants who exercised more frequently tended to experience more restorative sleep. The findings build on previous research connecting physical activity with non-REM sleep, a stage that includes the deep sleep essential for physical recovery and healthy brain function.

Chris Corral, who recently earned a master's degree in health behavior and health education from UT Austin and co-led the study, explained that deep sleep is especially crucial during the early hours of the night. During this period, the body carries out many of the processes that help it recover from the day's physical and mental demands.

Participants who were active more often spent more time in these valuable stages of sleep.

"That's exactly what you want," Baird mentioned.

"Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression.".

Industry observers note that one particularly encouraging finding was how little exercise appeared to be necessary. Among the young adults studied, as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity per day was associated with better sleep.

That level of effort does not require an exhausting workout. According to the researchers, moderate to vigorous activity involves breathing harder than usual while still being able to carry on a conversation. On a scale of 1 to 10, the effort would feel like approximately a 6.

Sources indicate that even gentler movement appeared to offer benefits. Regular walking and taking breaks from sitting to stand were also associated with healthier sleep patterns and a more positive mood the following day.

Better Sleep Linked to Improved Mood and Energy.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extended beyond what happened during the night. Participants who exercised more regularly also tended to feel more energetic and experience less stress the next day.

"We saw that more non-REM sleep was tied to better next-day mood and energy," Baird noted.

Sources indicate that this connection is notable because sleep affects far more than whether someone feels rested in the morning. Deep sleep helps the brain and body recover, supporting processes involved in memory, emotional regulation, and overall health.

It has been revealed that previous research has repeatedly linked physical activity with improved sleep, while better sleep itself is associated with greater well-being. However, many earlier investigations took place in controlled laboratories and examined relatively brief periods, sometimes measuring the effects of exercise over a single night.

The UT Austin team wanted to understand how these relationships played out under ordinary living conditions, where exercise habits, sleep schedules, and daily activities can vary considerably.

Recent findings suggest that to accomplish this, the researchers used wearable fitness trackers to collect information over several months. The Fitbit data allowed them to compare participants' movement habits with their sleep patterns over time, offering a more detailed picture of how everyday activity relates to sleep quality and next-day mood.

Although the findings reveal meaningful associations, the observational approach does not establish that exercising more frequently directly causes improvements in sleep.

Why Daily Exercise May Be Better Than Weekend Workouts.

The results also raise questions about how people should organize their exercise routines.

Current recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization call for approximately 150 minutes of moderate physical activity each week. However, those recommendations do not require people to distribute their activity evenly across the seven days.

According to recent reports, for some, meeting a weekly exercise target means taking long walks or completing challenging workouts on Saturday and Sunday. Others prefer shorter sessions spread throughout the week.

The UT Austin findings suggest that the second approach may offer particular advantages for sleep, although more research is needed to determine whether daily activity is better than completing an equivalent amount of exercise on fewer days.

"Our results suggest that daily movement may be better for sleep than doing it all on the weekend," Corral remarked.

If further studies confirm the importance of exercise frequency, the findings could eventually influence how public health organizations advise people to stay active.

"Current guidelines don't reflect the importance of frequency for sleep health," Baird noted. "Having this kind of data allows us to start thinking about whether they should.".

What Better Sleep Could Mean for Brain Health.

The possible implications go well beyond feeling more alert after waking up.

According to recent reports, during sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions, including strengthening memories and removing waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Healthy sleep is also closely connected with emotional well-being and long-term physical health.

Recent findings suggest that "Sleep is when your brain stores memories, clears waste and resets," Corral explained. "Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression.".

The research is part of UT Austin's Whole Communities -- Whole Health initiative, an interdisciplinary program that works with communities to investigate factors influencing health and well-being.

Sources indicate that the team is now preparing to examine whether the same patterns appear in a larger and more diverse population through the Whole Communities -- Whole Health five-year cohort study. This next phase will help researchers determine whether the findings extend beyond college students to people of different ages and physical activity levels.

For now, the results point toward an accessible way to potentially improve sleep: Make physical activity a regular part of everyday life.

Rather than focusing exclusively on long workouts or ambitious fitness goals, people may benefit from finding small opportunities to move throughout the day. A brief exercise session, a walk, or simply getting up regularly instead of remaining seated may all contribute to healthier routines.

"You don't need to run marathons," Corral remarked. "Just moving a little each day helps. Light activity counts too. Doing something is better than doing nothing.".

Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#103334. Industry News: How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2119 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How India Is Embracing Social-Emotional Learning

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students.
  • Sources indicate that india’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions.
  • The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When educators feel emotionally and physically supported, they’re in a much better position to support their students. In India, where the relationship between teacher and student has long been central to education, caring for teachers is essential to sustaining that connection.

Sources indicate that india’s education system comprises over 1 million government schools and more than 82,000 government-aided institutions. Serving approximately 167 million children, India administers the world’s largest education system. Increasingly, educators around the world recognize that social-emotional skills like navigating conflict and building healthy relationships are just as essential as academic learning—and India’s own national policies have begun to reflect that shift.

The 2020 National Education Policy calls social-emotional learning (SEL) “a critical aspect of any student’s holistic development.” That’s supported by the National Curriculum Framework, which recognizes the importance of fostering stronger student-teacher relationships to accomplish this approach.

According to recent reports, aditi Ramanthan, a high school biology teacher with almost 20 years of experience, has seen the shift toward more thoughtful discussion and implementation of SEL throughout her time teaching. However, as SEL becomes a more important part of education, the question is not only how to support students, it’s how to support the teachers who are being asked to help them develop these skills.

From this perspective, the future of teaching in India may not be defined only by new curricula or digital tools, but by whether schools can become places where the hearts of teachers are systematically cared for, so they can, in turn, care for the hearts of children.

Sources indicate that “The primary need is psychological safety,” says Ramanathan. “Instead of constantly viewing teachers as being emotionally self-sufficient, creating a space where they can ask for help.”.

In recent years, SEL implementation in India has been widely championed and led by school counselors, with educators throughout grade levels recognizing it as something that should be on par with academic curriculum.

“In India, social-emotional learning is just beginning to come into focus,” says Ramanathan. “Until recently, it wasn’t really part of mainstream conversations in schools, but now we’re starting to talk about it more seriously.”.

Sources indicate that ramanthan argues that while SEL has become more widely accepted in recent years, it should be treated as a basic professional requirement for teachers, much like first-aid training, if it’s to be successfully implemented in schools. While schools routinely prepare educators to respond to physical emergencies, far less attention is given to the emotional crises that are likely to unfold in their classrooms. She suggests that SEL training should be universal for teachers, equipping them to understand and respond to students’ inner lives, not just their academic performance.

“We are not trained for SEL, and I wish we were,” claims Ramanthan. “We’re given first aid training, but we are not given SEL training, and I think all of us should do SEL training.”.

Sources indicate that in a former position, Vrinda Loiwal, founder of the Center for Social Emotional Learning, designed SEL assessments for students, primarily in government-run schools. Once every three months, she would enter classrooms across the country to see how SEL was being interpreted, taught, and assessed.

“One of the challenges to children’s well-being is that even if you teach one SEL standalone lesson once a week, it has to be embodied in the math class, and the English class, and on the playground, and in the messaging all around the students,” Loiwal states. “I believe that there’s very little impact that can come with just a standalone lesson.”.

Recent findings suggest that inconsistency is another challenge. Loiwal explains that about a decade ago, the Delhi school district adopted a upcoming SEL program—and after years of teacher training and evaluation, they had evidence that what they were doing was working. However, in recent years with a new government in place, the program was scrapped and replaced.

Sources indicate that while on paper these new policies tick all the boxes for SEL implementation, when it comes to policy, introducing new required methods every few years disrupts the system just as educators begin to find their footing. They are constantly forced to recalibrate their entire approach, which creates an immense amount of pressure on the educators who are already overwhelmed and stretched thin for time.

Recent findings suggest that “All the teacher training now has to happen all over again and in a slightly new way because now there’s a new curriculum,” indicates Loiwal. “We all agree that you have to teach addition and subtraction in math, but we don’t yet all agree that we have to teach SEL skills or build SEL cultures. These are early efforts, and they’re building. Then the politics change and it feels like two steps forward, one step back.”.

At the Kaveri Group of Institutes in Pune—which includes schools that range from elementary to graduate level—leaders see the strain up close. Teachers are being asked to carry the weight of being disciplinarians, counselors, curriculum experts, and cultural bridges with no real pause in the day to breathe or reflect.

Industry observers note that “An educator is expected to teach, educate, to discipline, to mold the child, to develop the child, to understand the parents, different stakeholders, all of that,” states Deepa Kajale, a consultant for Kaveri. “It’s really overwhelming for the educator to put up with all these kinds of responsibilities.”.

Kajale is a play- and arts-based therapist and school psychologist who has worked with many interventions and iterations of SEL frameworks to foster inclusive, emotionally safe environments. While policymakers are increasingly viewing SEL as essential and not optional, Kajale and her colleagues at Kaveri are attempting to bridge the gap between newly required written frameworks and implementation.

For example, at the Kaveri Gifted Education and Research Center—which aims to identify and nurture gifted students across India—school counselors offer confidential spaces for teachers to talk about both professional and personal struggles like burnout and family stress, and they encourage educators to speak with counselors as a form of ongoing support, rather than viewing reaching out as a last resort.

It has been revealed that devasena Desai, Associate Director for Kaveri Counseling, Empowerment and Gifted Unit since 2014, says that in addition to offering wellness sessions where they talk about nutrition and menopause, they also celebrate Teacher’s Day. Each year on September 5, they host a large gathering complete with awards to teachers for creativity and innovation, live music, and loud cheering as colleagues are honored.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Additionally, she says one of the most fruitful decisions they made is to offer outsourced counselors from other districts for their educators to speak to.

According to recent reports, “Because sometimes you don’t want to talk to the person whom you bump into every day,” says Desai. “Maybe you’re not comfortable and we want to respect that. There are people who wouldn’t mind and there are some people who wouldn’t want to, so that option is there.”.

Along with this more formal support, Kaveri has built in daily rituals of connection, including listening circles where they talk about how to manage varying responsibilities, as well as more sensitive topics like overload and grief.

“What we have introduced in the last two years is talking about trauma, talking about grief, talking about single parenting, blended families, and how to embrace that,” states Desai.

Sources indicate that according to a paper published in June of this year that studied SEL in Nagaland, India, successful implementation requires specific teacher and parent engagement as well as dedicated training and resources. Additionally, SEL had to be contextually adapted and culturally aligned with local traditions.

The team at Kaveri understands the importance of cultural relevance when introducing these practices and often draw on concepts like guru and dharma to restore social meaning to the role of the teacher. The ideal of the teacher as a guru or a guide for both knowledge and character still carries significant cultural weight.

Unfortunately, that ideal can collide with the modern reality of rapid policy shifts, new technologies, and a workforce made up largely of women juggling caregiving at home and expanding expectations at work.

Industry observers note that “Within the professional identity, there is a personal identity with roles, responsibilities, and a lot to take care of as a woman,” says Kajale. “So that adds up to the emotional exhaustion that an educator goes through.”.

According to recent reports, guru is a Sanskrit word meaning “heavy” or “weighty,” used to describe a spiritual teacher or guide who dispels ignorance and leads a student toward self-realization. Rather than abandon the guru ideal as outdated, Kaveri is reclaiming it for the 21st century by rooting teacher support in Indian knowledge systems. In this model, SEL is not just a borrowed framework or a one-off workshop; it’s woven into listening circles, parenting programs, and grief support; and practiced by using a model of wellness that treats educators as whole human beings—body, breath, mind, and spirit.

“We believe that for the holistic development of a person, you have to be very balanced with all your koshas,” notes Malati Kalmadi, secretary of Kannada Sangha Public Trust.

In the Panchakosha model from Vedantic philosophy, there are five koshas—or the “five layers of human existence”—including the Annamaya (physical), Pranamaya (energetic), Manomaya (psychological), Vigynamaya (intellectual), and Anandamaya (spiritual). This holistic journey begins with the Annamaya Kosha, focusing on our physical essence through the food we consume. Beyond the visible body lies the Pranamaya Kosha, the vital energy that governs our internal systems—respiratory, circulatory, and nervous.

Achieving equilibrium in these physical and energetic layers is the foundation for mastering the Manomaya Kosha, or the mind. The Vijnanamaya Kosha connects us to our intellect and discernment, while the Anandamaya Kosha is our innermost peace.

Unlike Western perspectives that often separate diet from cognition, the Panchakosha model believes that the food we eat deeply influences the nature of our thoughts, inextricably linking our physical choices to our emotional and mental clarity.

Industry observers note that parents play a vital role in supporting this intentional shift back toward traditional models; Kaveri is working to more deliberately support parents in lifting these inherent values. In addition to the Mindful Parenting Program Workbook they created in collaboration with the Greater Good Science Center’s Parenting Program, they have taken it upon themselves to create additional parenting modules to help parents address the evolving cultural landscape and shifts between millennials, Gen-Z, and Generation Alpha.

It has been revealed that to help parents, students, and educators align their koshas, they have experts speak to them about how to switch from “fast food” to “slow food,” helping them become more conscious of what they put into their bodies. One of their team members also went to Bangalore for a training on traditional Indian well-being therapies to provide an alternative to Western medicine.

Sources indicate that “We feel that once we are able to get all these things into place, then the wisdom and the thoughts actually move towards spirituality,” says Kalmadi. “Our aim is taking the child towards this track for a better society.”.

While there is no single clean-cut path forward to create schools and districts grounded in SEL, educators across India are already showing that change is possible. By caring for teachers as whole people and drawing on both new research and longstanding cultural traditions, schools can create environments where educators feel supported to care for themselves, their students, and one another.

In that sense, the future of SEL in India may begin not with another mandate, but with a growing recognition that when we care for the people who teach, we strengthen the entire educational community.

According to recent reports, “There is slowly a conversation happening between parents, and schools, and teachers, which earlier was not happening consciously, but now we are doing it very, very consciously,” notes Kalmadi. “This is proving to be very beneficial for the entire educational ecosystem.”.

Industry observers note that emily Brower is the Education Editor at the Greater Good Science Center and an Associate Producer of The Science of Happiness podcast. In her role as Education Editor, she has covered educator well-being around the world, exploring the experiences and challenges of educators in Ukraine, Singapore, and Spain. Previously, as a music and travel journalist, she contributed to publications including Pure Nowhere, Fifty Grande, and KCPR, covering destinations across Southern and Northern California and the Central Coast. Emily earned a B.S. in Journalism with a concentration in Public Relations and a minor in Art History from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo. She later received her master’s degree from the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

Latest Update: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice

📅 12 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain?
  • Sources indicate that the findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China.
  • Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.

Sources indicate that the findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.

Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.

How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging.

At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.

It has been revealed that scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an vital player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.

In a recent development, earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.

The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.

Sources indicate that they discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other key types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.

To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.

According to recent reports, the results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.

Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.

Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days.

The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?

Sources indicate that to find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.

Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.

In a recent development, their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.

In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.

These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.

But the researchers also uncovered an vital clue about how Menin produced these effects.

A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue.

When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.

It has been revealed that amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other vital functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.

According to recent reports, D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.

It has been revealed that further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.

Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.

This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.

To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.

The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.

According to recent reports, however, there was an notable distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.

That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.

Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging.

Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.

In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.

That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.

In a recent development, another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has crucial protective functions in brain cells.

An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.

The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells revealed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.

These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.

New Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways.

Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.

Sources indicate that in a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.

According to recent reports, another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.

Together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.

Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?

The possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.

According to recent reports, A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.

More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.

In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.

Industry observers note that these findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.

Sources indicate that there are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.

For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.

Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?

Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.

Why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?

It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.

Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.

"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," remarked Leng.

Industry observers note that leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes.".

In a recent development, the growing body of evidence points toward a potentially crucial shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.

In a recent development, the possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results showed that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, stated:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very notable to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This remarked, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially notable, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

According to recent reports, “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” states René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and new spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

“Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” indicates Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”.

Hsu indicates he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this new era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”.

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over.

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026.

Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the latest boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

In a recent development, the 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a newly introduced acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Visitor at West Bund Art & Design 2026.

Courtesy of West Bund Art & Design.

Dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she indicates.

Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

It has been revealed that also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, says that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

It has been revealed that he suggests that the growth of latest art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang says, adding that Shanghai remains an key entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

Sources indicate that hsu indicates the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”.

Love in the Time of Dinosaurs

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1824, studying a set of large fossil bones discovered in a quarry near Oxford two centuries earlier, the English theologian, geologist, and paleontologist William Buckland kept looking at the fragment of the lower jaw.
  • He christened it Megalosaurus — the first named dinosaur — and set out to compose a complete account of the ancient beast.
  • Because nobody knew what dinosaurs looked like, he needed an exceptional scientific illustrator whose unbridled imagination and disciplined draughtsmanship could enflesh the bones of the mysterious creature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1824, studying a set of large fossil bones discovered in a quarry near Oxford two centuries earlier, the English theologian, geologist, and paleontologist William Buckland kept looking at the fragment of the lower jaw. Something didn’t add up. As he examined it more closely, he realized these were not the remains of an elephant, as previously thought, but of an enormous carnivorous reptile with no analogue in the fossil record or in the living world.

He christened it Megalosaurus — the first named dinosaur — and set out to compose a complete account of the ancient beast.

Because nobody knew what dinosaurs looked like, he needed an exceptional scientific illustrator whose unbridled imagination and disciplined draughtsmanship could enflesh the bones of the mysterious creature. Taken by a particularly excellent drawing of the jaw of an extinct hyena, he obtained a letter of introduction to the artist, tucked it into his coat pocket, and boarded a coach across Devonshire, hoping to be received.

In a recent development, william took one book to accompany him on the long ride — a weighty fresh volume by paleontology founding father Georges Couvier, summarizing his pioneering research on the fossil bones of quadrupeds. With gaping disbelief, he watched another passenger take out that same book and begin paging through it. The conversation was inevitable and the realization quick: She was the artist he was traveling to meet. Cuvier himself had sent her the book in gratitude for her contribution.

In a recent development, perhaps because she had lost her mother while still an infant, Mary Morland had grown up fascinated by deep time, by the slow-burning beauty of minerals, by the way fossils immortalized the ephemerality of the flesh. After devouring Couvier’s books as a teenager, she taught herself draughtsmanship and unlearned what her culture had told her she could be: Determined to become an artist of science, she sent her specimen illustrations to Couvier himself.

It has been revealed that the venerable scientist was so taken with the young woman’s work that he published it alongside his studies. Word spread across the scientific community and soon she was illustrating other books and modeling rare specimens in leather.

It has been revealed that unlike most women of her time, whose standard path to subsistence was marriage, Mary could now make a living by her own work. If she married, it would only be for love. Her love was the science of time: She kept drawing paleontological specimens, grew an impressive mineral collection, became a fossil geologist herself.

According to recent reports, by the time she met William that day on the coach, she was an old maid in her late twenties and one of the era’s most esteemed scientific illustrators. They started on the dinosaur work immediately.

Within a year, Mary Morland was Mary Buckland. Their home became a miniature Alexandria of science books, light pouring in from candle-holders made of ichthyosaurus vertebrae, fossils lining every sideboard. Their dining room housed a menagerie of frogs and snakes. Guinea pigs ran regularly across the table. A pony occasionally rode past, a laughing child on its back.

One of their surviving children would later recount that Mary not only illustrated William’s studies but, with her “great mental powers, habits of perseverance and order, tempered by excellent judgment,” she “gave to them a polish which added not a little to their merit.”.

Recent findings suggest that despite their fourteen-year age difference, she outlived him by just over a year, channeling her bereavement in studying marine bryozoans — coral-like saltwater creatures — with her daughter. Hours before her death, Mary was still bent over her microscope, entranced by a new specimen.

Mary and William were buried alongside one another, their entwined fossils to be discovered by some paleontologist of the far future: What is love if not the mutual belonging of our passions and our bones.

Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins.
  • Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located.
  • "So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.

Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.

"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease.".

Sources indicate that researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.

Recent findings suggest that their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.

The findings were published in Nature.

Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain.

To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.

According to recent reports, the team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.

The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.

Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.

"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," states D'Angelo.

Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps.

The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.

In a recent development, one striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.

"This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal key features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.

Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids.

Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered upcoming insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.

According to recent reports, when researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.

It has been revealed that the cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, revealed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an vital component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.

These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.

According to recent reports, "Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," notes Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs.".

A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease.

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.

By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.

The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.

"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

How To Instantly Read Someone’s Personality With One Question

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.
  • Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, said:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.

Sources indicate that the idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality. On one side, fine silk in fluid motion, pale yellow, soft and light. On the other, solid sculpted gold forms with architectural weight. The identity holds both at once: garments described as vulnerability and armor, built for a woman who commands the room with quiet power. Nothing shouts. The yellow field does the talking, and the black line work sits on it with total control.

It has been revealed that the wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house. Thin, delicate strokes carry the lightness, while high contrast serifs give the letters their structure. The detail that holds it together is the ligatures: internal connective strokes, clearest in the N, I, E and R, link the characters the way woven silk holds a thread, so the name reads as one continuous piece. A construction frame reveals the letters PA on black, with guide bars and notes on the straight serifs and the joins between letters.

Sources indicate that the moth mark works the same way. It is built from four overlapping geometric forms, a line drawing of the Bombyx mori silk moth, the living link between the Persian name Parnia, a canvas of fine silk, and the sculpted gold the house stands for.

Sources indicate that the system stays physical wherever it lands. The moth mark sits alone on a pale yellow tile, then repeats as a woven petal pattern in yellow, gold and tan. The brand book opens in a black ring binder: a yellow page carries the wordmark embossed into the paper, facing a white page headed "Essence of allure." The same yellow carries the shopping bag, the wordmark pressed into the paper along the bottom edge, with black ribbon handles.

At street level the system scales up without changing its voice. A tall yellow banner hangs on a red brick building beside a panel with the moth mark, and the closing collage pulls the whole world together: moth tile, beaded gown detail, patterned envelope, shopping bag, the wordmark on yellow, and the line "Presence without the noise." It is a quiet luxury, stated once and left alone.

#103326. Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1446 w)
